food.text: Chenla existed in Indochina from the late 6th to the early 9th century, following the earlier kingdom of Funan. Its wealth came from wet-rice agriculture and from the mobilization of manpower, rather than from subsistence farming as in the past. Productive lands were donated to temples, where slaves worked the fields and helped the temples generate revenue.

The Shailendra dynasty emerged as rulers in Java in the 8th century. Although famous as a seafaring power across maritime Southeast Asia, they also relied on intensive rice cultivation on the Kedu Plain of Central Java.
Chenla built an extensive irrigation system across its territory. This system produced rice surpluses that made up the bulk of the kingdom's trade.

By the early 7th century, Cambodian society was shifting from a trading economy to an agrarian one. Coastal trading centers from the Funan period were collapsing, while inland agrarian centers emerged.

art.text: By the 7th century, Khmer sculpture began to drift away from its Hindu influences. It had drawn on pre-Gupta models for its Buddhist figures and Pallava models for its Hindu figures. Through constant stylistic evolution, it developed its own originality, which by the 10th century can be considered complete.

The Shailendra dynasty of Java extensively promoted Buddhist art from around the 8th century. That art found its strongest expression in the vast Borobudur temple. Buddhism flourished across Southeast Asia between the 5th and 13th centuries.

The Khmer Empire covered much of mainland Southeast Asia from the early 9th century. During that time it developed a sophisticated architecture. The structures of its capital city, Angkor, are the best example.

Khmer sculpture soon went beyond religious representation, which became almost a pretext for portraying court figures in the guise of gods and goddesses. It also became a means and an end in itself, a kind of testing ground for stylistic refinement.

Most of Southeast Asia introduced dance into its courts. Cambodian royal ballet was represented in the early seventh century, before the Khmer Empire, and was highly influenced by Indian Hinduism. The Apsara Dance, famous for strong hand and feet movement, is a great example of Hindu symbolic dance.

Behind Khmer sculpture's stylistic refinement, one can imagine small groups of intellectuals and artists at work. They competed among themselves in mastery and refinement as they pursued a hypothetical perfection of style.

war.text: In 938, Ngô Quyền led the Vietnamese forces in the Battle of Bạch Đằng River against the Chinese Southern Han dynasty. His men planted iron spikes under the river, attacked as the high tide hid them, and held the enemy fleet in check for hours until the tide fell and the spikes impaled the Chinese armada. They then followed with ferocious fire attacks and annihilated hundreds of giant warships, killing the Southern Han navy and the Prince of Southern Han. The victory led to the Ngô dynasty, a semi-independent Vietnamese dynasty that ruled from 939 to 968.

The rebel leader Triệu Quang Phục made his headquarters on an island in a vast swamp. From this refuge he could strike without warning, seize supplies from the Liang army, and slip back into the labyrinthine channels of the swamp.

In 545, Emperor Wu of Liang sent troops to recapture the region from the Early Lý dynasty. In 546 the Gia Ninh fortress fell, and Lý Bí and his army fled and waged guerrilla warfare against the Liang.

Around 930, northern Vietnam was militarily occupied by the Southern Han but treated as a vassal state of the Later Tang Dynasty, called Tĩnh Hải quân. Under Lord Protector Dương Đình Nghệ, it launched a full blown military campaign for independence, while China was weakened by civil war.

In 905, Khúc Thừa Dụ of the Khúc clan took advantage of turmoil in China, seized power from the weakened Tang, and appointed himself Jiedushi. This established a degree of autonomy for Vietnam. The Huang Chao rebellion had weakened the Tang in the late 9th century.

The An Lushan rebellion, from 755 to 763, caused massive upheaval in the Tang dynasty. Early in the rebellion, tribal people set up at least seven kingdoms between Annan and the Tang empire, cutting off contact until the Tang reclaimed the region in 758.

Owing to Vietnam's fragmented terrain and long coastline, most military forces that fought there favoured maneuvers by boat. Warfare in the period beginning with the 938 defeat of the Southern Han combined amphibious and land assaults, and small-scale coastal and border raids were frequent.

General Võ Nguyên Giáp, a much later Vietnamese revolutionary, said that Vietnamese concepts of protracted warfare were born in the tactics of Triệu Quang Phục. He named surprise offensives, night attacks, and hit-and-run tactics.

The Chinese could make no headway against Vietnamese guerrilla-style warfare, and the indecisive period lasted until 557. Then the Liang dynasty was hit by the Hou Jing rebellion, and the famous general Chen Baxian's skills and troops were needed at home to quell a revolt.

In the late 8th century, Phùng Hưng raised an army and took control of Annan. He and his son Phùng An briefly overtook Guangzhou in maritime trade. In 803, Phùng An willingly surrendered control of Annan to a newly appointed Tang jiedushi.

literature.text: Chinese characters, known as chữ Hán, came to Vietnam during the thousand years of Chinese rule from 111 BC to 939 AD. Texts in Vietnam were being written in chữ Hán by the 10th century at the latest.
For a millennium before the tenth century, Vietnam was ruled by various Chinese dynasties, so much of its written work was in chữ Hán. Works in this script were called either Hán văn or văn ngôn.
Chữ Nôm, created around the tenth century, let writers compose in Vietnamese using native characters. These characters were coined by using Chinese radicals.

Chữ Nôm blended chữ Hán with unique Vietnamese characters to write the Vietnamese language. It may have been used as early as the 8th century, but concrete textual evidence only dates to the 13th century.
Shailendra dynasty inscriptions from 8th and 9th century Java were written in three languages, Old Javanese, Old Malay, and Sanskrit, using either the Kawi script or the pre-Nāgarī script.

The Nôm script suited Vietnamese literature better, leading to poetic forms like Lục bát and Song thất lục bát. It also allowed Vietnamese reduplication to be used in poetry. From the 10th century, a minority of literary works were composed in it.

In 2017, Japanese archaeologists working on a 9th century shipwreck in Quang Ngai, in Champa, found ceramic shards with inscriptions in Indic script. The inscriptions refer to a place near what is now Hormuz, Iran.
Inscriptions on some of the Quang Ngai shipwreck fragments end with a pentagram or a hexagram. Islamic historian Do Truong Giang interpreted this mark as the Seal of Solomon.

science.text: Borobudur, a Buddhist temple in Java, was built of gray andesite-like stone in nine stacked platforms, decorated with 2,672 relief panels and originally 504 Buddha statues. Its hidden foot carries 160 panels showing cause and effect, with blameworthy acts from gossip to murder set beside their punishments, and the pains of hell beside the pleasures of heaven. Of the 504 Buddha statues, over 300 are damaged, mostly headless, and 43 are missing, since heads have been looted by personal collectors or acquired by museums.

By the 7th century, the maritime empire of Srivijaya, based in Sumatra, had developed complex technologies to exploit maritime resources thanks to its strategic location. This technological advantage helped Srivijaya dominate much of western Maritime Southeast Asia for centuries.

The Shailendra dynasty, which emerged in 8th-century Java, relied on intensive rice cultivation on the fertile Kedu Plain of Central Java to sustain its population, while also covering the plain with Buddhist monuments, including the colossal stupa of Borobudur.

The Prambanan temple compound in Java, completed in the mid-9th century, originally consisted of 240 individual temple structures, including a central tower rising 47 metres high. It remains the largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia, reflecting the advanced stone construction techniques of its time.

The earliest temples at Mỹ Sơn in Champa, central Vietnam, were built from wood, including timber logs. This wooden complex burned down in a fire around 535 or 536 CE, during the reign of Rudravarman I, and King Sambhuvarman, who took power in 572, rebuilt the site in the 7th century.

The reliefs at Borobudur in Java also depict an 8th to 9th-century wooden double outrigger sailing ship used by the Javanese people, now known as the Borobudur ship. Similar vessels remained in use for coastal trade in East Java until at least the 1940s.

Some historians once thought the Borobudur ship might be a later Majapahit vessel, but Majapahit's main ships, the jong, malangbang, and kelulus, did not have outriggers, unlike the ship carved at Borobudur. This distinguishes the Borobudur ship as a distinct type of Javanese vessel.

Other named vessels from the era include the samvau, recorded in the 683 CE Kedukan Bukit inscription in Sumatra and ancestor of the modern sampan, and the lancang, mentioned in two Old Balinese inscriptions dated 896 and 923 CE. The Borobudur ship itself is found only at the Borobudur temple, unconnected to any Sumatran or Malay record.

politics.text: By the 7th century, the seaborne empire of Srivijaya had emerged by conquering and subjugating neighbouring thalassocracies such as Melayu, Kedah, Tarumanagara and Mataram. Its polities controlled the sea lanes of Southeast Asia and the maritime trade routes between India and China.
In 544, Lý Bí defeated the Liang dynasty and proclaimed himself emperor. He named his country Vạn Xuân, meaning "Myriad Spring", and built the Trấn Quốc Pagoda in Hanoi.

Chinese rule over northern and central Vietnam lasted, in its main phase, until 939 AD, when the Ngô dynasty was established. Vietnamese historiography traditionally dates the start of this period to 111 BC, when the Han dynasty annexed Nanyue.

Between the 8th and 11th centuries, the Medang Mataram kingdom flourished in Central Java under the Sailendra dynasty, which was also the ruling family of Srivijaya. The dynasty's kings became ardent patrons of Buddhism.

Lý Bôn's 544 declaration as Emperor of Yue followed a personal grievance. The Liang court had rejected him and Tỉnh Thiệu as non-elite, and he found no avenue for advancement in the Liang dynasty's administrative system. He only declared his emperorship after failing to obtain an official appointment there, having rebelled when the governor Xiao Zi extorted the people of Jiao. The Liang later defeated him; Lao tribesmen he sought refuge with betrayed him, and his head was sent to the Liang court.

A Sanskrit inscription dated 775 AD was found at Nakhon Si Thammarat in southern Thailand. One side names a great monarch of the Śailendra dynasty, and the other records Buddhist sanctuaries founded by a king of Srivijaya. It is seen as testimony to Srivijaya's expansion onto the Malay Peninsula.
politics.source_title: Sanskrit inscriptions in Maritime Southeast Asia

politics.text: The Sailendra king Panangkaran reigned from 760 to 780, and during his reign Mahayana Buddhist influence rose in central Java. The grand stone mandala of Borobudur was later completed during the reign of Samaratungga, who ruled from 819 to 838.

Chinese annals record that Rudravarman, the last king of Funan, reigned from 514 to 545 and sent many embassies to China. Funan might then have been conquered by another kingdom called Zhenla around 627 CE, ending it.

Lý Nam Đế was assassinated in 547, and his elder brother Lý Thiên Bảo became the de facto ruler of Vạn Xuân. Lý Thiên Bảo died of an illness in 555 and left no heirs, so the military and officials elected Triệu Quang Phục as leader and de facto ruler.

Triệu Quang Phục's election was disputed by other family members of Lý Nam Đế. He claimed rightful succession through court officials, the military and the people, while the Lý relatives insisted leadership must pass by hereditary right as they remained the ruling family in name.

The Tugu inscription, linked to Tarumanagara, records a water project on the Gomati river ordered by King Purnawarman in the 22nd year of his reign. The river was straightened and widened to avoid flooding in the wet season and to serve as irrigation in the dry season.
politics.source_title: Sanskrit inscriptions in Maritime Southeast Asia

politics.text: Ngô Quyền won the Battle of Bạch Đằng River against the Southern Han in 938 by planting iron spikes beneath the water, holding the Southern Han navy in check until the tide fell and the spikes impaled its ships, then attacking with fire; the Southern Han navy and the Prince of Southern Han were killed, and he founded the Ngô dynasty. However, his dynasty failed to control chieftains, and he never gained Chinese acknowledgement of his legitimacy. In 951 Đinh Bộ Lĩnh began a rebellion from his mountainous home region of Hoa Lư, and by 966 the country was split among 12 warlords fighting one another.

Emperor Wen of Sui sent an envoy to Vạn Xuân demanding that Lý Phật Tử submit as a vassal state, but Lý refused. In 602, Lý Phật Tử bribed Lệnh Hồ Hy, the governor of Qi Zhuo, and the angry Emperor Wen of Sui had Lệnh Hồ Hy executed for corruption. He then ordered general Liu Fang to invade Vạn Xuân with 100,000 troops, and Lý Phật Tử surrendered, marking the beginning of renewed Chinese domination in Vietnam.

philosophy.text: Indian religious ideas shaped how Southeast Asian rulers understood power. Chenla's first ruler Vīravarman adopted the idea of divine kingship and used the concept of Harihara, a syncretistic Hindu god that embodied multiple conceptions of power. His successors kept the tradition.

Indianized kingdoms turned small indigenous polities led by petty chieftains into major kingdoms led by a Maharaja, with statecraft akin to India's. This process gave birth to the Khmer Empire, the Sriwijayan kingdom on Sumatra and the Mataram kingdom, among others.

Chenla's rulers followed the Manusmṛti, the Laws of Manu for the Kshatriya warrior caste. In doing so they conveyed the idea of both political and religious authority. It shows an Indian ethical code being used as a guide for kingship in Southeast Asia.

Hindu thought spread east to the Indonesian Srivijaya empire and the Cambodian Khmer Empire. It carried the Hindu synthesis, which had merged orthodox Brahmanical thought with unorthodox elements from Buddhism and Jainism.

Buddhism in Southeast Asia has two main traditions, Theravada and Mahayana. Theravada took hold mainly in Burma, Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and southern Vietnam, while Mahayana took root primarily in maritime Southeast Asia. Mahayana is thought to have spread from both China and India.

culture.text: Between the 5th and the 13th century CE, Buddhism flourished in Southeast Asia. By the 8th century, the Buddhist Srivijaya kingdom based in Sumatra had emerged as a major trading power in central Maritime Southeast Asia.

Local rulers converted to Hinduism or Buddhism and adopted Indian religious traditions. They did so to reinforce their legitimacy, elevate their ritual status above fellow chiefs and facilitate trade with South Asian states. They periodically invited Indian Brahmins into their realms.

Most Southeast Asian people were originally animist, engaged in worship of ancestors, nature and spirits. These belief systems were later supplanted by Hinduism and Buddhism, especially in coastal areas that came into contact with the Indian subcontinent.

Muslim traders were visiting and living in Southeast Asia as early as the 7th century, mainly through the port town of Barus on the west coast of Sumatra. Dutch historian J. C. Van Leur estimated that Arab colonies had formed in Barus by 674. The tombstone of Syekh Rukunuddin, who died in 672, is further evidence.

Chenla, the successor of Funan, existed from around the late 6th century until the early 9th century. Its first ruler Vīravarman adopted the idea of divine kingship and the concept of Harihara, a syncretistic Hindu god that embodied multiple conceptions of power.

The Khmer Empire was established by the early 9th century in a mythical initiation and consecration ceremony by its founder Jayavarman II at Mount Kulen in 802 CE. His successors continued the Hindu devaraja tradition.

Historians such as Frederic Pain, Keith W. Taylor and Michael Churchman argue that Vietnamese culture came into being during the millennium of Chinese rule. They hold that it emerged as a distinct culture that was recognizably Vietnamese after the collapse of the Tang dynasty during the 10th century.

Shaivism spread into Southeast Asia via the Bay of Bengal, Indochina, then the Malay Archipelago. It led to thousands of Shiva temples on the islands of Indonesia as well as in Cambodia and Vietnam, co-evolving with Buddhism in the region.

Chenla's successors obeyed the Manusmṛti, the Laws of Manu for the Kshatriya warrior caste, which conveyed the idea of political and religious authority. Chenla also adopted the Sanskrit epigraphic system of the south Indian Pallava and Chalukya dynasties.

Dutch historian J. C. Van Leur estimated that Arab colonies were already formed in Barus by 674. In 2017 Indonesia established the Titik Nol (Zero Point) Monument in Barus, recognizing the city's role in the spread of Islam in Indonesia.

The Khmer king Jayavarman II, who lived about 800 to 850, founded a cult identifying the king with the Hindu god Shiva. He established a capital at Angkor in central Cambodia. Shiva was the god symbolising destruction and reproduction, one of a triad with Brahma and Vishnu.
culture.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia
